The farm-productivity reader is useful when a productivity workbook needs to
be analysed without losing the source table, method, geography, or financial
year that gave an observation its meaning. This vignette uses the small
package fixture shipped at `inst/fixtures/workbooks/farm-productivity.xlsx`.
The fixture is package-owned synthetic data: it is structurally faithful to
the workbook profile, but its values are not an official ABARES release.

## Read a local workbook

Local paths are deterministic and do not require discovery or network access.
Use a cache below `tempdir()` for a vignette, test, or batch job rather than
writing to a home or project directory.

```{r setup}
library(readagau)

farm_file <- system.file(
  "fixtures", "workbooks", "farm-productivity.xlsx", package = "readagau"
)
stopifnot(nzchar(farm_file), file.exists(farm_file))

farm_cache <- tempfile("readagau-farm-productivity-")
dir.create(farm_cache)

productivity <- read_farm_productivity(
  release = farm_file,
  adjustment = "all",
  view = "reported",
  cache_dir = farm_cache
)
```

The result is a `farm_productivity_data` tibble (also inheriting from
`agau_data`). A compact view of the semantic fields is usually more useful
than printing the complete provenance payload:

```{r farm-preview}
productivity[
  seq_len(min(8L, nrow(productivity))),
  c(
    "table_id", "table_title", "commodity", "geography", "period",
    "period_status", "method", "unit", "value"
  )
]
```

Every row also carries `release_id`, `source_sheet`, `source_note`, `sha256`,
`parser_version`, `observation_key`, and the shared observation-contract
fields. For a local file, `release_id` is checksum-qualified unless an
explicit `release_id` and `release_date` are supplied. The file name and file
modification time are not treated as official release identity.

## Method profiles and filters

The `method` column separates conventional, climate-adjusted, and interim
adjustment observations. The interim label is retained when it is present in
the source; `adjustment = "all"` is the way to inspect the complete profile.
The reader also accepts `"conventional"` and `"climate_adjusted"` as method
filters, plus optional `industries` and `geography` filters.

```{r method-profile}
method_profile <- as.data.frame(
  table(productivity$method, useNA = "ifany"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
names(method_profile) <- c("method", "observations")
method_profile
```

For a focused method view, the same local source can be read again with a
filter. This is still an offline parse; the cached workbook bytes are reused.

```{r conventional-filter}
conventional <- read_farm_productivity(
  release = farm_file,
  adjustment = "conventional",
  view = "reported",
  cache_dir = farm_cache
)

conventional[
  seq_len(min(6L, nrow(conventional))),
  c("table_id", "commodity", "geography", "period", "method", "value")
]
```

## Financial-year semantics

Simple financial-year labels are normalised to inclusive dates. For example,
`1999-00` and `1999-2000` both describe `1999-07-01` through `2000-06-30`.
Malformed ranges fail closed; named or multi-year summary labels remain
undated rather than being guessed. Inspect both the source label and the
normalised bounds when joining to another time series.

```{r period-bounds}
period_view <- productivity[
  !is.na(productivity$period_start),
  c(
    "table_id", "period", "period_start", "period_end", "period_basis",
    "method"
  )
]
period_view
```

The parser records `period_status` separately from the date bounds. A period
can therefore be dated without being silently reclassified as an estimate or
forecast.

## Provenance, failures, and live data

`source_note`, `source_provider`, `rights_status`, `sha256`, and
`retrieved_at` are provenance fields, not replacements for source attribution.
The fixture above is safe for reproducible examples; it should not be quoted
as an official estimate. For an official release, pass the exact local asset
or an exact release ID and retain the returned hash.

Passing a workbook from another product is a typed failure rather than an
attempt to guess a table profile. The following uses another packaged fixture
only to demonstrate the failure contract:

```{r typed-failure}
wrong_product_file <- system.file(
  "fixtures", "workbooks", "crop-national.xlsx", package = "readagau"
)
failure <- tryCatch(
  read_farm_productivity(wrong_product_file, cache_dir = farm_cache),
  error = function(e) {
    list(class = class(e)[1L], message = conditionMessage(e))
  }
)
failure
```

The first class is an `agau_*` condition (normally
`agau_validation_error` for an incompatible workbook). Code that needs to
recover should branch on the condition class, not on a translated message.

The package can discover current official assets when `release = "latest"`
or when a reader is called without a local path, but that path needs network
access and may change as the publisher updates its landing page. Keep live
examples opt-in and use a managed cache. The guard below is intentionally off
for CRAN and ordinary vignette builds; set `READAGAU_RUN_LIVE=true` in an
interactive session only after checking the source's current terms.

```{r live-productivity, eval=TRUE}
if (interactive() && identical(Sys.getenv("READAGAU_RUN_LIVE"), "true")) {
  live_productivity <- read_farm_productivity(
    release = "latest",
    view = "canonical",
    cache_dir = farm_cache
  )
  utils::head(live_productivity)
}
```

The offline fixture path above is the supported reproducible workflow for
tests, package checks, and documentation. Network failures, changed source
schemas, and missing assets should be handled as explicit package conditions
and investigated with the returned release and asset metadata.
